text.p: Republican Bob Dole launched his 96-hour, non-stop "victory tour" on Friday in a hectic bid to pull off a spectacular upset victory over President Bill Clinton in Tuesday's election.

The marathon, stopping only for showers in hotels, will take Dole to at least 14 states before Election Day and test not only whether voters will oust Clinton from the White House but also the 73-year-old Dole's endurance.

He started out at college rallies in Columbus and Ashland, Ohio, where he received sendoffs from former Republican presidents George Bush and Gerald Ford in the first time Bush, Ford and Dole had campaigned together.

High above Ohio on his plane from the first stop in Columbus to Ashland, Dole proclaimed:"It is high noon - 96 hours and counting. 96 hours to victory. We're on the way. The clock is ticking. One, two, three, four five. We're on the way to the White House. Haaang on."

Here at Ashland University, where Las Vegas nightclub singer Wayne Newton joined the entourage that included Ohio Gov. George Voinovich, Dole pounded Clinton again over running what he has sees as an unethical White House.

"A president should be a source of inspiration. This president is a source of cynicism. He has led an administration without a compass and without a core. We deserve an ethical White House. We must demand an ethical White Houos. And next Tuesday, we must vote for an ethical White House," Dole said.
He promised if elected to establish a White House office of ethics "to guarantee that the business of the people is not compromised by politics."
How do you feel? Dole was asked as he left his hotel on Thursday morning for a rally at Capital University, Columbus. "Feel great. Not so sure about tomorrow morning," he said.
By Saturday morning, Dole will have been up most of 24 hours with stops in Ohio, Michigan, New Jersey, Pennsylvania.

Dole, far behind in polls, was feisty and told the Columbus rally that his 96 hours was serious. "We're not doing this to punish the media," he said, in a lighthearted reference to what he calls the "liberal media."
"We have four big days...we're going to win this election...this is a fight for America, to elect a president we can trust, and one who will give us an economy that will give us hope," he said.

But the thrust of his talks to students in Columbus and Ashland was a steady attack on what he calls ethical lapses in the White House, and the controversy over Democratic Party acceptance of questionable contributions from people with links to Indonesia, Taiwan and other foreign interests.
He noted that Republicans had the Watergate scandal under Richard Nixon and said the party learned its lesson.
"We took a licking, we reformed but we didn't go far enough," said Dole, who ridiculed Clinton's call for a campaign finance reform commission to overhaul campaign laws.
"The administration is in the midst of a growing scandal involving a flow of foreign money into the Democratic Party that bought access to the White House," Dole said.
"So now Bill Clinton decides to talk about campaign finance reform," he said. "What we have seen from this administration in the last few weeks is the reason we need campaign finance reform."

Dole, who recommended a campaign reform commission as a senator six years ago, said: "I suggested it again two weeks ago in New Hampshire -- so I'm glad the president's making progress." He asked Clinton to accept "common sense ground rules" for a commission, such as barring contributions from non-Americans.
Both Bush and Ford adopted the Dole line of attack against alleged misdeeds in the White House.
Bush brought up the White House collection of sensitive FBI files on Republicans by White House security office aides and said when he was president he never saw an FBI file.
Ford urged voters to fight apathy and vote, saying that if he had woon Ohio -- a major battleground state where Clinton leads now -- he would have beaten Jimmy Carter for the presidency in 1976.
